The article theorized while they do have a DNS, typing in IP addresses may be easier for those without typing skills.
I got so excited when I read it, and then I realized it happened in 2013

What I find interesting is that several (or maybe even all?) of the IP addresses are in a local address block (10..., 192.168.., 172.16..*) It is as if 3 different IT departments installed an intranet at one company and just tagged it together. LAN parties are better organized than this.
It's pretty funny, but the 10.x.x.x space can allow over 16.7 million unique IPs alone.

True, it is a Class A space, that can support 128 (through subnetting if I remember correctly) x 16.7 million addresses. My point was not that they don't have enough IP addresses to go around with this way, but just that they are not standardized in one address space. For a totalitarian regime, you would expect standardization to be top priority.
I guess the Dear Leader wants to make damn sure these devices cannot get outside North Korea in case someone accidentally plugs the wrong cable into the wrong switch, hehe.

This is very interesting. For one, no DNS. Why they chose not to use it, I have no idea.

What is perhaps even more interesting is that those are all non-routable IP ranges. 192.168.x.x - 10.x.x.x - 172.16.x.x . This means that these addresses can't be routed directly to the general internet.

North Korea is designed entirely like the inside of a corporate or home network.

More like a home network. Every corporation I've worked for had DNS. They develop their own in house pirates and reverse engineer, so DNS has to be an option. I wonder why leave it out? Maybe so that users don't know how to use the general internet? When they see a google.com they don't know what to do with it.
